analysis_note: All pre-1900 excerpts are plain-language renderings of public-domain sources.

documents.source_line: Christopher Columbus, letter to the Spanish monarchs reporting his first voyage
documents.sourcing_note: A Genoese captain writing to his royal sponsors; purpose is to report success and secure continued funding. His glowing description of wealth serves his need to justify the voyage.
documents.text_or_description: I have discovered many islands rich in gold, spices, and all things men desire. The people are gentle and generous, and I took possession of these lands for our King and Queen. With a little help, great riches will follow.

documents.source_line: Bartolomé de Las Casas, Dominican friar, in A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies
documents.sourcing_note: A Spanish friar writing to the Spanish court; purpose is to denounce the encomienda system and demand reform. His horror stories are meant to shock the crown into action, which shapes his emphasis.
documents.text_or_description: The Christians laid hands upon the Indians with a cruelty never before seen. For gold they slew men, women, and children without mercy, tearing babes from their mothers and dashing them against the stones. Whole islands were left empty of people.

documents.source_line: Florentine Codex: Nahua account of the smallpox epidemic, given by survivors to the friar Bernardino de Sahagún
documents.sourcing_note: Indigenous survivors speaking through a Franciscan friar; purpose is to record the catastrophe. The description of social collapse shows disease as the most devastating force of the exchange.
documents.text_or_description: A great plague broke out among us. It covered the body with sores from head to foot. Many died of hunger, for none could cook food or bring water. The dead lay unburied in the houses, and none dared enter to carry them out.

documents.source_line: The New Laws, issued by the Spanish Crown
documents.sourcing_note: Imperial legislation addressed to colonial officials; purpose is to assert royal authority over the conquistadors and regulate conquest. Shows the crown responding to the very abuses described in Document 2.
documents.text_or_description: We command that henceforth no Indian shall be made a slave for any reason. Those held in unjust servitude shall be set free, and the grants of Indian labor given to the first conquerors shall return to our Crown.

documents.source_line: Antonio de Morga, Spanish colonial official, in Sucesos de las Islas Filipinas (Events in the Philippine Islands)
documents.sourcing_note: A Spanish colonial official in Manila writing a history of the islands for Spanish readers; purpose is to record the colony’s commerce and government. Writing as an insider to the Manila trade, his inventory of Chinese goods bought with American silver documents the global circuit: New World silver flowing east to pay for Asian manufactures.
documents.text_or_description: Every year ships arrive from China laden with raw silk, fine silks in many colors, porcelain, and other wares. The Chinese merchants sell their goods and carry the proceeds back to China in silver — minted coin and bars — linking the mines of Spanish America to the markets of Asia through Manila.

documents.source_line: Casta painting from New Spain, depicting a mixed-race family
documents.sourcing_note: Painted by an anonymous colonial artist for Spanish viewers; purpose is to classify the new racial hierarchy of the colonies. Shows both the cultural mixing and the rigid social ranking the exchange produced.
documents.text_or_description: The painting shows a Spanish father, an Indigenous mother, and their mixed-race child, labeled with the colonial term for their caste. Such paintings catalogued dozens of racial mixtures in a strict social order.

documents.source_line: Map of the triangle trade across the Atlantic
documents.sourcing_note: A modern educational map; purpose is to illustrate the system. Shows how the exchange created a new forced migration that tied three continents into a single commercial circuit.
documents.text_or_description: The map shows three routes: European manufactured goods to Africa, enslaved Africans carried to the Americas, and American plantation goods such as sugar and tobacco shipped to Europe.

prompt: Using the documents and your knowledge of world history, evaluate the most significant effects of the Columbian Exchange on societies in the Americas and Afro-Eurasia in the period c. 1450-1750.

analysis.complexity: Multiple paths: weigh demographic catastrophe (Docs 2, 3) against economic integration (Docs 5, 7) and social transformation (Doc 6); corroborate Spanish cruelty across Docs 2 and 4 (the crown's laws respond to the friar's charges); qualify 'significance' by region and by who experienced the effect.
analysis.sourcing: Doc 1 (audience/purpose: a captain justifying his voyage to his sponsors); Doc 2 (purpose: a reformer shocking the court into action); Doc 3 (point of view: Indigenous survivors); Doc 5 (context: a colonial official's history recording the Manila trade — American silver flowing east).

rubric_map.contextualization: Situate the exchange within European maritime expansion, the Reconquista's crusading mentality, the Ottoman control of eastern trade routes pushing Europeans seaward, and the pre-existing American and Afro-Eurasian societies it disrupted.

evidence.describe: All seven describable; strongest: Docs 2, 3 (human cost), Docs 5, 7 (economic systems), Doc 6 (social order).
evidence.outside: Outside evidence: the demographic collapse of Indigenous populations (up to 90 percent in some regions); the transfer of crops (maize, potatoes, sugar) and animals (horses, cattle); the Potosí silver mines and the Manila galleons; African kingdoms' participation in and resistance to the slave trade.
evidence.support: 'Demographic/social catastrophe most significant': Docs 2, 3, 6, 7. 'Economic integration most significant': Docs 1, 5, 7. 'Political/administrative effects': Doc 4.

rubric_map.thesis: An arguable thesis takes a position on 'most significant' with a line of reasoning, e.g., the sample below.

sample_thesis: The most significant effect of the Columbian Exchange was demographic and human: the catastrophic population collapse caused by disease and exploitation in the Americas, and the forced migration of enslaved Africans, reshaped societies more profoundly than the new trade in silver and crops, because the loss and movement of peoples determined who would labor in, govern, and inherit the new Atlantic world.
title: The Columbian Exchange
